extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially indie authors) considering hiring a sensitivity reader
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, experience-based guidance on selecting, hiring, and working with sensitivity readers for fiction manuscripts, with concrete lessons from the author's engagement with two providers. Emphasizes matching, deliverables, contracts, communication, and author responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shop around
rubrics_metrics.description: Shop around if you can afford it (or ask around if you have fellow writers hiring sensitivity readers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author hired two different companies to compare critiques and warns that hiring only one could give a misleading impression of the value of sensitivity services. Review multiple providers, read bios/reviews, and compare sample outputs when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do your homework; don't jump at the first reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't jump at the first sensitivity reader you come across, even if you think they’re the perfect match. Do your homework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check reader bios, company policies, sample deliverables, turnaround, and reputation. Contracts sometimes limit what you can learn publicly about a reader, so extra diligence is warranted when you're spending hundreds of dollars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand indirect interactions and follow-up limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand interactions with your reader will likely be indirect, and you may be limited on how much follow up you’re allowed to request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many companies use intermediaries (no direct contact between author and reader) which can restrict Q&A and quick clarifications. Plan accordingly—be prepared to use the company as the go-between and expect written-only communication in many packages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book readers ahead for series work
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find an editor you like and you’re writing a series, consider booking them for multiple engagements ahead of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers' schedules can become chokepoints. The author booked multiple future reads to guarantee availability and deadlines; stagger bookings reasonably so you can actually produce the next manuscript before the reader's slot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide questions or flagged areas with the manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Salt & Sage encourages writers to send along questions or comments with their manuscripts. Take advantage of this if your reader allows it!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point reviewers to scenes, plot lines, or character presentations that feel off to you; this functions like a targeted Q&A and can yield richer, more useful responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be detailed and specific in your questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be detailed and specific in your questions to your reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since many interactions are text-based and limited, vague questions lead to unhelpful answers. The author notes that a 4-page list of questions produced a 13-page answers document—specificity yields specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be respectful and humble in interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: When it comes to working with your reader, be respectful and humble. You’re paying for a service—but treat the reader kindly and follow contract terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not stalk, attack, harass, or personally confront a reader over disagreement. If you disagree with feedback, handle it through the company. Remember critiques are about the manuscript, not you personally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the emotional toll on readers
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find a good reader match for your manuscript, you are likely asking someone to relive personal and painful experiences. Your unintended missteps will trigger an unpleasant reaction in your reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before rejecting critique, consider the emotional labor the reader invested. Be considerate when responding; their work may require them to recount trauma or discrimination to explain problems in your manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers are not gatekeepers or representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity readers are neither gate keepers nor givers of permission. They are individuals providing their subjective opinions about your manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat readers as official representatives of a community. Use their input as valuable perspective, but remember the author must accept final responsibility for the impact of the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider price vs. depth tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a price vs detail tradeoff: you can pay more for a far more detailed critique or accept a lighter read at base price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author paid an extra $200 for a more detailed critique after reviewing an 11K-word sample of the reader's feedback. Ask for samples of a reader’s work and confirm what level of detail is included at each price tier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check contract clauses about publicity and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts often include clauses that forbid publicly referencing the company or reader without explicit permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy likely protects readers from harassment but can limit your ability to publicly endorse or advertise a reader. Be aware of and respect these clauses, and request permission if you want to promote your reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect intermediaries and limited direct contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Many editing companies use intermediaries between clients and readers (i.e., no direct contact between the two).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model reduces scheduling/communications logistics and protects readers, but it can be frustrating. Some companies/packages (Deluxe Developmental edit) may include calls; check package details if direct contact matters to you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment terms vary (upfront vs deposit; payment methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Payment policies differ: some require payment in full and up-front; others take a deposit then the balance on delivery. Accepted payment methods can also differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Company One required full payment (PayPal only), Salt & Sage charged half up-front and balance on delivery. Confirm payment schedule and method before committing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliverables and formats differ widely
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliverables can range from a short summary critique to extensive reports and in-line manuscript comments plus Q&A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Company One delivered a 2.5-page Word doc with critique; Salt & Sage/Sachiko provided a 60-page PDF plus an in-line commented Word doc and the option for a single round of unlimited questions. Ask for examples of typical deliverables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/background match matters for quality of feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: A reader’s lived experience, cultural background, and genre familiarity influence the depth and usefulness of their feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sachiko (female, half Japanese, half white, urban fantasy fan) produced more specific cultural insights than Reader One, whose critique was more generic. Prioritize readers who both understand the culture and the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity feedback can prompt developmental improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity and sensitivity feedback often leads to developmental changes—plot, setting, and character adjustments—not just wording fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a single comment led the author to research Little Tokyo history and improve world-building; correcting sensitivity issues improved narrative credibility and triggered broader rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider combined sensitivity + developmental edits and loyalty discounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies may offer combined sensitivity/developmental edits at lower combined cost and provide loyalty discounts for repeat customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author was offered a combined package for a prequel and later received a 10% loyalty discount. Discuss package options and discounts if you plan multiple engagements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors retain final authority; readers can explicitly permit authors to keep choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Good readers give honest feedback but explicitly acknowledge 'this is your story' and let authors make the final choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sachiko regularly reminded the author that her feedback was advisory and that he could choose whether to adopt suggestions; this helps maintain creative agency and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract for second reads and ongoing involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractor readers typically do not continue working on a manuscript up to final published version unless you pay them for additional reads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want a reader to re-check revisions or final proofs, budget for a follow-up/read round or develop a system (e.g., summaries of major changes) to keep the reader apprised between separate paid engagements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify formatting and pagination expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Formatting mismatches can cause issues (e.g., critique referencing page numbers that don't match submitted manuscript).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow submission formatting guidelines but be aware readers may reformat; clarify whether feedback will reference your file's pagination and provide guidance on how to map comments back to your manuscript if formats change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm turnaround times and expedite options
rubrics_metrics.description: Turnaround estimates vary (e.g., 3–4 weeks) and companies may offer faster delivery for additional fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Company One quoted 4 weeks, Salt & Sage quoted 3 weeks but could move the deadline earlier; confirm start dates, realistic delivery windows, and extra-cost expedited options before hiring.
